name: Triangle length
seoTitle: Triangle length Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Triangle length: work out side (c) from the angle α and the side. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: side (c) is what the Triangle length calculator works out, and it gets there from the angle α and the side. That makes it useful for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Triangle length calculator work?
sections.html:
The Triangle length calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports side (c) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the angle α and the side (b).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Triangle length calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Side (c)=side (b) × the cosine of (angle α) + the square root of ((side (a) ^ 2) − (side (b) ^ 2) × (the sine of (angle α), 2))
Side (c)=side (a) × the cosine of (angle β) + the square root of (-(side (a) ^ 2) × (the sine of (angle β), 2) + (side (b) ^ 2))
Side (c)=the square root of ((side (a) ^ 2) − 2 × side (a) × side (b) × the cosine of (angle γ) + (side (b) ^ 2))
Angle β=-angle α − angle γ + PI

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Angle α = 10 deg, Side (a) = 30 mm and Side (b) = 30 mm. Working through the relationship above gives Angle β = 10 deg, Angle γ = 160 deg and Side (c) = 59.088 mm.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Angle β = 10 deg, Angle γ = 160 deg and Side (c) = 59.088 mm should be roughly the size you expected from Angle α = 10 deg and Side (a) = 30 mm.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Triangle length calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the angle α and the side — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Triangle length calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns side (c), derived from the angle α and the side. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Triangle length calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the angle α and the side, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter angle α in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Angle α opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Angle β = 10 deg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Triangle length calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
